title: Oil Prices Extend Rally After Ship Attacks and US-Iran Talks Collapse
excerpt: Brent crude heads for a sixth straight day of gains as attacks near the Strait of Hormuz and a breakdown in ceasefire talks keep energy markets on edge.
body:
• Brent crude rose to $89.08 per barrel, heading for a sixth consecutive day of gains, after attacks on two ships near key Middle East shipping routes and a breakdown in US-Iran ceasefire talks.
  • Vessel traffic through the Strait of Hormuz fell to a one-week low of just eight ships on Tuesday, down from 125-140 per day before the conflict.
  • Iran told Reuters there are no discussions to extend the ceasefire because Tehran considers the deal to have had no start date.
  • US crude inventories rose sharply by 9.1 million barrels, according to API data, potentially offsetting some supply-side pressure if confirmed by official figures.

Oil prices climbed in volatile trading on Wednesday after attacks on two commercial vessels reinforced fears of sustained disruptions to Middle East energy supplies, even as a surprise build in US crude stockpiles tempered gains.

Brent crude futures rose 17 cents, or 0.2%, to $89.08 a barrel by mid-morning in London, heading for a sixth straight session of gains. US West Texas Intermediate crude added 20 cents to $83.40, on track for its fifth consecutive daily increase. Both benchmarks had surged more than $1 earlier in the session before pulling back.

Strait of Hormuz Under Pressure

The United States and Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthi movement reported separate attacks on shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and the Bab el-Mandeb Strait on Tuesday — two of the world's most critical chokepoints for oil and gas exports. The attacks follow weeks of escalating tensions that have repeatedly disrupted traffic through the waterways.

Shipping data painted a stark picture of the disruption. The number of vessels transiting the Strait of Hormuz fell to a one-week low of eight on Tuesday. Before the US-Iran conflict, 125 to 140 vessels passed through the strait daily, carrying roughly one-fifth of the world's oil supply.

Ceasefire Talks Hit an Impasse

Prices regained momentum after a senior Iranian source told Reuters there were no discussions between Tehran and Washington to extend their ceasefire. Iran's position, according to the source, is that the deal had no start date and therefore there was nothing to extend — a stance that undercuts weeks of diplomatic signals suggesting the two sides might find a path back to negotiations.

"The risk is that this escalates to levels seen early in the war, where neighboring countries and their energy infrastructure are also targeted."

— Analyst note, via The Wall Street Journal

The breakdown follows a turbulent July that saw the US-Iran memorandum of understanding effectively collapse. President Donald Trump declared the agreement "over" after Iran struck three commercial ships in the strait, prompting the US to reimpose a naval blockade on Iran's coastline. Brent crude posted a 24% gain in July, its largest monthly rise since the early months of the conflict.

US Inventory Build Provides a Counterweight

Market focus shifted briefly to US supply fundamentals after American Petroleum Institute data showed crude stockpiles rose by approximately 9.1 million barrels, far exceeding analyst expectations. Gasoline inventories fell by 1.5 million barrels and distillate stocks declined by 596,000 barrels.

If confirmed by the Energy Information Administration's official report due later Wednesday, the crude build could ease immediate concerns about supply tightness, according to analysts at Haitong Futures. However, the geopolitical risk premium continues to dominate pricing.

Longer-Term Outlook Remains Elevated

The EIA has projected that significant disruptions to Middle East crude supplies will persist through the end of 2027, forecasting that Brent crude will average $86.81 a barrel in 2026 and WTI will average $80.88.

In Libya, the country's National Oil Corporation said all fires at fuel storage tanks in the Zawiya oil complex were under control, providing some relief on a separate supply concern. But with Hormuz traffic at a fraction of pre-war levels and diplomatic channels between Washington and Tehran effectively frozen, the path of least resistance for oil prices remains upward.
